abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Paracetamol (PCM) is extensively metabolized in the liver via glucuronidation, sulfation, and oxidation. Although oral and intravenous PCM are commonly used interchangeably, a comprehensive evaluation of PCM metabolism across both routes is lacking. This study aimed to characterize the full pharmacokinetic (PK) profiles of PCM and its metabolites following oral and intravenous administration, accounting for presystemic and systemic metabolism. Concentrations of PCM, PCM‐glucuronide (PCM‐GLU), PCM‐sulfate (PCM‐SUL), PCM‐cysteine (PCM‐CYS), and PCM‐mercapturate (PCM‐MER) were pooled from three clinical studies, involving 53 adults with obesity and 16 adults without obesity (18–65 years, 53–198 kg). A semi‐physiological population PK model was developed with nonlinear mixed‐effects modeling, incorporating intestinal and liver compartments, and enterohepatic recirculation. A semi‐physiological PK model incorporating presystemic and systemic hepatic metabolism captured PK of PCM and PCM‐SUL following oral and intravenous administration. Intestinal oxidative metabolism for PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER and enterohepatic recirculation for PCM‐GLU were added to capture their full PK profiles. The estimated fraction of PCM absorbed was 0.745 (95% CI 0.699–0.792), with extensive first‐pass metabolism and faster metabolite formation after oral than after intravenous administration. This semi‐physiological population PK model identified both hepatic and intestinal presystemic metabolism of PCM, as well as enterohepatic recirculation of PCM‐GLU. Oral administration of PCM results in faster metabolite formation than intravenous dosing, mainly for the oxidative metabolites. This modeling approach may support the quantification of presystemic and systemic metabolism, which can be relevant for oral and intravenous dosing of drugs metabolized by multiple pathways.

sec.p: Keywords: drug metabolism, enterohepatic recirculation, paracetamol, pharmacometrics, presystemic

list-item.p:
What is the current knowledge on the topic? ○
Paracetamol (PCM) is extensively metabolized via glucuronidation, sulfation, and oxidation. Although its pharmacokinetics have been widely studied, a comprehensive evaluation of PCM metabolism following oral and intravenous administration is lacking.

What question did this study address? ○
How can the full pharmacokinetic profiles of PCM and its metabolites following oral and intravenous administration be quantitatively evaluated, with a focus on the contributions of presystemic and systemic metabolism?

What does this study add to our knowledge? ○
Following oral administration, the fraction absorbed was 74.5%, and PCM metabolism was faster than after intravenous administration, particularly for the oxidative pathway. Enterohepatic recirculation of PCM‐glucuronide was identified, influencing PCM and metabolite profiles, with a particular impact following oral administration.

How might this change drug discovery, development, and/or therapeutics? ○
This semi‐physiological population pharmacokinetic model of PCM identified relevant presystemic oxidative metabolism in the gut and enterohepatic recirculation of PCM‐glucuronide. Application of a semi‐physiological population pharmacokinetic modeling approach to drugs undergoing multiple pathways allows identifying novel information on both presystemic and systemic metabolism that can be used to optimize dosing after oral and intravenous administration.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Paracetamol (acetaminophen, PCM) is a widely used analgesic and antipyretic drug. It is extensively metabolized in the liver, mainly via glucuronidation (55%), sulfation (30%), and oxidation by cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes (5%–10%) [1, 2, 3, 4]. The oxidation pathway generates the toxic metabolite N‐acetyl‐p‐benzoquinone imine (NAPQI). Under normal conditions, this compound is detoxified by glutathione conjugation to form the harmless metabolites PCM‐cysteine (PCM‐CYS) and PCM‐mercapturate (PCM‐MER). When PCM is given at therapeutic doses, glutathione can sufficiently neutralize NAPQI. However, when glutathione is depleted (e.g., in cases of PCM overdose or malnutrition), this leads to increased accumulation of NAPQI, which can lead to liver failure.

PCM is rapidly absorbed after oral administration and undergoes first‐pass hepatic metabolism. Its pharmacokinetics have been extensively studied in diverse populations, including individuals with obesity [5], pregnant women [6], neonates [7], and older adults [8]. Several factors, including genetic polymorphisms and hepatic enzyme activity, contribute to interindividual and interethnic variability [4]. Patient weight is an important driver for PCM metabolism. Patients with obesity (BMI ≥ 30 kg m−2) have higher hepatic blood flow and increased expression of CYP2E1—the enzyme involved in the oxidative metabolism of PCM and the formation of NAPQI [5]. As a result of increased CYP2E1‐mediated oxidation, glucuronidation, and sulfation, patients with obesity have an increased PCM clearance, whereas they also have a higher volume of distribution (Vd), leading to lower systemic PCM levels after standard dosing [5, 9]. In addition, patients with obesity show earlier and higher peak concentrations of PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER after the first dose. Despite these changes, the relative contribution of each metabolic pathway remains comparable to that of individuals with normal weight [5]. In support of additional factors influencing the PK of PCM and its metabolites, studies have suggested the presence of CYP2E1 in the intestines [10] and enterohepatic recirculation of PCM‐GLU in rats [11, 12], where deglucuronidation of PCM‐GLU and subsequent reabsorption of PCM in the gut were observed. These observations highlight the complex interplay between physiological factors and PCM metabolism and underscore the importance of studying presystemic and systemic processes across different routes of administration.

Although a recent physiologically–based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model studied PCM PK following both oral and intravenous administration, it did not account for metabolite formation [13]. Additionally, previous studies examined intravenous [5] and oral [9] PCM metabolism separately. Hence, a comprehensive combined evaluation of PCM metabolism following oral and intravenous administration to study presystemic and systemic metabolism is lacking. Therefore, this study aims to study the PK of PCM and its metabolites after oral and intravenous administration in patients using a semi‐physiological population PK approach.

sec.title: Study Design and Population
sec.p: In this pooled study, data were obtained from three independent clinical studies on the PK of PCM and metabolites (see Table 1). Study 1 (PAPAYA Study) was a clinical trial conducted in the Netherlands, including patients with obesity planned to undergo a laparoscopic Roux‐en‐Y gastric bypass and healthy participants without obesity. Participants were excluded if they were pregnant, had liver disease, or had received PCM within 24 h prior to the study. Before participation, all participants provided written informed consent. This study was approved by the medical ethics committee of Erasmus Medical Center (NL70329.078.19) and the local scientific committee of Albert Schweitzer Hospital (2019–084). The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and the Medical Research Involving Human Subjects Act (WMO) of the Netherlands. All included patients and healthy participants received 1000 mg of oral PCM (2 tablets of 500 mg from Teva, dispersed in 50–100 mL water prior to administration). Blood was drawn pre‐dose and at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 24 h following administration of PCM. Blood samples for PCM and metabolite analyses were collected in sodium EDTA tubes and centrifuged at 3000 g for 10 min. Plasma was stored at −80°C until analysis. Blood samples for liver function tests were collected in lithium heparin tubes before PCM administration, after 6 h, and after 24 h. For this PK analysis, only results from patients with obesity before surgery and healthy participants without obesity were included.

sec.p: Study 2 was previously conducted in patients with obesity who were scheduled to undergo laparoscopic Roux‐en‐Y gastric bypass in the United States [9]. All patients received a single dose of 1500 mg oral PCM. For this PK analysis, only results from patients before surgery were included.

Study 3 was a previously published study performed in the Netherlands, including patients with obesity planned to undergo a bariatric surgical procedure (laparoscopic Roux‐en‐Y gastric bypass or gastric sleeve) and patients without obesity undergoing oral and maxillofacial surgery [5]. All patients received 2000 mg of intravenous PCM just prior to the surgery. After 8 h, patients could receive PCM according to the standard postoperative pain protocol. Consequently, data from Study 3 included samples obtained after multiple doses of intravenous PCM. Detailed study designs and patient characteristics for Study 2 and Study 3 have been described previously [5, 9].

sec.title: Drug Assays
sec.p: PCM, PCM‐GLU, PCM‐SUL, PCM‐CYS, and PCM‐MER were measured using high‐performance liquid chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS). The analytical details of Study 1 were previously described by Flint et al. [14], and those of Study 2 were described by Chen et al. [9], and of Study 3 by Van Rongen et al. [5].

sec.title: Structural Model Development
sec.p: The starting point for model development was the previously published model on the basis of intravenous PCM data from Study 3 [5]. In short, this model consisted of a one‐compartment model for PCM and PCM‐GLU, a combined one‐compartment model for PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER, and a two‐compartment model for PCM‐SUL, with linear eliminations for all metabolites. To incorporate oral data and account for potential route‐specific differences in PK, the model was extended in three steps.

As a first step, an oral depot compartment with first‐order absorption was added to allow estimation of the fraction absorbed (Fa) and the absorption rate constant (ka). All other structural features and model assumptions were retained from the original intravenous model [5].

In the second step, it was assessed whether presystemic metabolism accounts for differences in metabolite profiles following oral and intravenous administration. For this step, a semi‐physiological model was implemented on the basis of Brill et al. [15], incorporating gut wall, portal vein, and liver compartments. Hepatic metabolism was parameterized using the well‐stirred liver model, where the hepatic extraction ratio (EH) was estimated by the parameters intrinsic hepatic clearance (CLH,int) and liver blood flow (QH). Intestinal metabolism was modeled by estimating the gut wall extraction ratio (EG), incorporating villous blood flow (Qvilli) and permeability clearance through the enterocytes in the gut wall (CLperm) [16]. The intrinsic intestinal clearance (CLG,int) was estimated as a fraction of CLH,int. Drug‐specific parameters such as fraction unbound and CLperm were obtained from the literature [17, 18] and implemented in this semi‐physiological model. The previously assumed fraction of PCM cleared unchanged [5] was excluded from this model because of its minimal contribution to total clearance. Full details about the drug‐ and system‐specific parameters and semi‐physiological equations can be found in Table S1.

In the third step, the inclusion of enterohepatic recirculation of PCM‐GLU was evaluated to explain potential differences in PCM and PCM‐GLU concentrations following oral and intravenous administration. A gallbladder compartment was incorporated on the basis of a modified version of the model described by De Winter et al. [19]. In this model, PCM‐GLU entered into the gallbladder. The gallbladder emptied at a periodic interval of 3 h, releasing PCM back to the gut wall via a first‐order reabsorption process. Release times of pulsated gall release were allowed to vary across the datasets, reflecting different fasting states (fasted in Studies 2 and 3 and no restrictions of fasting in Study 1). This model assumed that all participants had an intact gallbladder and biliary system.

Body size metrics, that is, total body weight or lean body weight (LBW), were initially retained from the original model of van Rongen et al. [5] and re‐evaluated in later phases of model development. To integrate these covariates into a model incorporating presystemic metabolism, the original LBW covariates previously applied to plasma clearances [5] were transformed to LBW covariates on CLH,int. LBW was calculated as described by Janmahasatian et al. [20].

sec.title: Model Selection and Evaluation
sec.p: Discrimination between models was guided by the precision of parameter estimates, shrinkages of omega and sigma (< 30%), a drop in objective function value (OFV, equal to minus two times log likelihood) with significance levels of p < 0.01 (decrease in OFV [dOFV] > 6.64) for hierarchical models, and parameter plausibility. Backward elimination was used to test whether a covariate could be left out (p < 0.01 or dOFV > 6.64). Goodness‐of‐fit (GOF) plots were stratified for route of administration (oral versus intravenous), study, and obesity status. To obtain parameter precision, sampling importance resampling (SIR) was used [21]. Internal model evaluation was further supported by stratified GOF plots and normalized prediction distribution error (NPDE) plots.

sec.title: Simulations
sec.p: To illustrate the differences in PCM and metabolite profiles between oral and intravenous administration, simulations were performed with the final semi‐physiological population PK model. Concentration‐time curves at steady state (1000 mg four times daily) were simulated following both oral and intravenous administration in patients with and without obesity. Curves of four typical patients from the dataset of Study 1 were simulated, that is, those with total body weights of 60 kg, 92 kg, 120 kg, and 150 kg. The 60 kg and 92 kg patients represent the lower and higher interquartile ranges of patients without obesity, whereas the 120 kg and 150 kg patients represent lower and higher weights than the median of patients with obesity. To illustrate potential differences between oral and intravenous administration, metabolite‐to‐parent area under the curve (AUC) ratios were compared.

sec.title: Software and Settings
sec.p: Population PK modeling was performed with NONMEM version 7.5 software (Icon Development Solutions, Hanover, MD, USA), applying the stochastic approximation expectation maximization with importance sampling (SAEM‐IMP) calculation method for parameter estimation. For model evaluation and data visualization, Pirana version 2.9.9 [22] and R version 4.0.5 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) were used. Dosing records and plasma concentrations were expressed in micromoles per liter, correcting for the differences in molecular weights between PCM (151.16 g mol−1), PCM‐GLU (327.29 g mol−1), PCM‐SUL (231.23 g mol−1), PCM‐CYS (270.30 g mol−1), and PCM‐MER (312.24 g mol−1) [5]. In contrast to the original mode by Van Rongen et al. [5], which used logarithmic data, this analysis used linear‐scale data. All concentrations below the lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) were removed from the dataset, as was previously described by Van Rongen et al. [5]. In addition to the data points excluded in the study by Van Rongen et al. [5], additional data points were removed from the datasets because of concentrations falling below the LLOQ [23]: 1 for PCM (0.1%), 5 for PCM‐GLU (0.7%), 3 for PCM‐SUL (0.4%), and 91 for PCM‐CYS & PCM‐MER (10.9%). Simulations were performed in NONMEM.

sec.title: Patients and Data
sec.p: Patient characteristics are summarized in Table 1. In total, 69 participants were included: 28 received PCM intravenously, and 41 received PCM orally. Notably, patients from Study 2 had comparable LBW and total body weight to those in the other studies but had a higher BMI.

Concentration‐time profiles of PCM and all metabolites are shown in Figure 1. From all observations, 13 individuals displayed double peaks in PCM concentration—9 after oral and 4 after intravenous administration—suggesting potential involvement of enterohepatic recirculation. In total, 782 PCM observations, 784 PCM‐GLU observations, 783 PCM‐SUL observations, and 766 PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER observations were available for analysis.

sec.title: Model Development
sec.p: The previously published compartmental model for intravenous PCM and metabolites [5] extended with an oral depot compartment, was first applied to the entire dataset to assess its predictive performance. This initial model showed that the formation of metabolites was faster following oral administration compared to intravenous dosing, most distinctively for PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER. The NPDE plot shows that PCM concentrations were overpredicted, whereas metabolites were underpredicted following oral administration (example in Figure S1). This discrepancy suggested a substantial role for presystemic metabolism.

To address presystemic metabolism, hepatic and intestinal clearance were incorporated as a second step in model development. The addition of the well‐stirred liver model alone—reparameterized into QH and CLH,int—improved model predictions for PCM and its PCM‐GLU and PCM‐SUL metabolites (data not shown), but showed considerable misfit for PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER during the first 2 h after administration. Therefore, intestinal oxidative metabolism was also included in the model, which further improved the model fit, particularly for PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER in the first 2 h following oral dosing (Figure S2). The ratio of CLG,int to CLH,int was 0.00474 (95% CI 0.0032–0.0069) in our study, which was comparable to previous findings in patients receiving midazolam, where this ratio was 0.0012 [15]. Unfortunately, no data about CLG,int of CYP2E1‐mediated metabolism are available. On the basis of mRNA and protein levels in different parts of the intestinal parts of humans [10, 24, 25], the low ratio of CLG,int to CLH,int was expected. Nonetheless, visual inspection of the NPDE plots suggested that the metabolite formation patterns still differed between oral and intravenous administration. Compared to intravenous dosing, oral dosing resulted in earlier conversions to PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER and reduced conversion to PCM‐GLU in the first 2 h after administration.

In the third model development step, enterohepatic recirculation of PCM‐GLU was incorporated to address the misspecification in the PCM and PCM‐GLU profiles, particularly for Study 1. Several secondary peaks in PCM concentrations were observed between 3 and 6 h after oral dosing. Implementation of enterohepatic recirculation of PCM‐GLU into the model strongly improved the fit for PCM and PCM‐GLU profiles (dOFV −143). In Study 1, where participants had no restrictions for fasting, gallbladder emptying was included at 1 h post‐dose and every 3 h subsequently. In contrast, emptying was delayed to 8 h post‐dose in Study 2 and to 6 h in Study 3, followed by 3‐h emptying intervals in both Studies 2 and 3. These differences are consistent with known physiological effects of fasting and food intake on gallbladder motility [26, 27]. The gallbladder emptying times were fixed to the indicated values with a fixed IIV of 131% derived from the model of de Winter et al. [19] to avoid estimation problems, most likely because of overparameterization. The fraction of PCM‐GLU routed into the gallbladder was fixed at 0.1, representing 10% of the total PCM‐GLU formed. A sensitivity analysis was conducted, and no improvement of model fit was observed with alternative fractions eliminated via the gallbladder.

Despite taking into account the dose differences, patients in Study 2 consistently showed higher PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER concentrations and slower elimination of metabolites than those in Study 1. Other body size metrics (i.e., BMI and total body weight) were tested to address these differences, but did not improve the model. To account for the differences between these oral datasets, study‐specific effects were added on: elimination clearance of PCM‐GLU (dOFV −51.0), PCM‐SUL (dOFV −40.9), and both the elimination clearance and CLH,int of PCM‐CYS and MER (combined dOFV −40.9). The addition of study‐specific covariates on Fa and ka did not improve the model, on the basis of OFV and GOF plots.

The final structural model is shown in Figure 2, incorporating gut wall, portal vein, and liver compartments, and enterohepatic recirculation. The drug‐ and system‐specific parameters, along with the model equations, are shown in Table S1. The corresponding model code can be found in Material S3. Table 2 shows the parameter estimates of the final model. Fa was estimated at 0.745 (95% CI 0.699–0.792), and the fraction escaping gut metabolism (FG) can be derived from Qgut/(Qgut + CLG,int × fUG). For illustration, FG can be calculated at 0.9995 for a male individual weighing 60 kg (LBW 40.8 kg) and 0.9992 for a male individual weighing 120 kg (LBW 71.5 kg). The overall bioavailability (F) is the product of Fa, Fg, and fraction escaping hepatic metabolism (FH): F = Fa·FG·FH (Table S1). Furthermore, ka was 0.0531 h−1 (95% CI 0.0415–0.0667), and Vd of PCM was 53.7 L (95% CI 50.2–57.0) for an individual with LBW 65.2 kg. The population CLH,int followed the expected hierarchy in metabolic routes, with glucuronidation being the most predominant pathway (CLH GLU 0.300 L min−1 [95% CI 0.278–0.327] for an individual with LBW 65.2 kg), followed by sulfation (CLH SUL 0.0667 L min−1 [95% CI 0.0608–0.0725] for an individual with LBW 65.2 kg), and oxidation (CLH CYS 0.0417 L min−1 [95% CI 0.0359–0.0486] for an individual with LBW 65.2 kg). The following covariates were identified to have a significant effect on PK parameters: LBW on Vd of PCM (dOFV −66.7), LBW on CLH GLU (dOFV −45.4) and on CLH CYS (dOFV −67.3), LBW on elimination clearance of PCM‐GLU (dOFV −36.9), and total body weight on Vd of PCM‐GLU (dOFV −54.4). We did not find a statistically significant effect of LBW on transit rate constant (ktr) nor on CLH,int of PCM to PCM‐SUL, as was previously identified in Study 3 [5].

sec.p: Despite model refinements, some misspecification remained in the final semi‐physiological population PK model. PCM‐SUL was slightly underpredicted in patients with obesity after intravenous administration, whereas predictions for individuals without obesity receiving oral PCM matched the observations. In the original model on the basis of intravenous data (Study 3) [5], a covariate of LBW on plasma clearance to PCM‐SUL was incorporated. However, adding LBW or total body weight as a covariate on CLH,int to PCM‐SUL did not resolve this discrepancy in the final model with oral and intravenous data.

sec.title: Simulations
sec.p: To illustrate the impact of the route of administration, concentration‐time profiles of PCM and metabolites were simulated in four representative male patients across the observed weight distribution (Section 2.4) under steady‐state conditions of 1000 mg four times daily, as shown in Figure 5. Following oral administration, metabolite formation was faster and led to earlier peak concentrations than following intravenous administration across all body weights. This effect was most prominent for oxidative metabolites (PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER). Because of rapid presystemic metabolism following oral administration, no delay in PCM‐GLU and oxidative metabolite formation was observed, whereas such a delay was apparent after intravenous administration.

sec.p: AUC0‐6 are depicted in Figure S4 in Supporting Information S2. The metabolite‐to‐parent AUC ratios for all metabolites were similar after oral administration and after intravenous dosing. For glucuronidation, the ratios ranged from 1.05–1.36 after oral administration versus 1.11–1.37 after intravenous dosing in individuals weighing 60 up to 150 kg. For sulfation, the ratios were 0.64–0.72 and 0.68–0.72, and for oxidation, 0.06–0.14 and 0.06–0.14.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: To date, a comprehensive evaluation of intravenous versus oral PCM metabolism is lacking. This study provided insights into how presystemic and systemic metabolism and enterohepatic recirculation contribute to differences in parent drug and metabolite exposure between the two routes. It enhances our understanding of the relative roles of hepatic and intestinal presystemic metabolism.

The following key observations emerged from this analysis. First, oral administration led to faster metabolite formation, particularly via the oxidative metabolites (PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER). Second, presystemic hepatic metabolism alone was insufficient to capture the rapid formation of PCM‐CYS & PCM‐MER, highly suggesting a role for intestinal oxidative metabolism. Although intestinal CYP3A metabolism has been shown for midazolam [15] and identified in PBPK modeling [28], this is, to our knowledge, the first time intestinal oxidative metabolism has been described. This is supported by the presence of CYP2E1 in human mucosa cells [10]. These results highlight the importance of presystemic metabolism—an effect that was underappreciated in prior PCM models that were developed using data upon either intravenous [5] or oral administration [29].

Third, following oral administration of PCM, relatively lower PCM‐GLU concentrations were observed in the first 2 h post‐dose compared to what is expected after intravenous administration. Together with the observed double peak PCM levels, this pattern indicated the occurrence of enterohepatic recirculation. Supporting this hypothesis, previous rat studies have demonstrated that PCM and PCM‐SUL formation were substantially delayed when PCM‐GLU was injected into more proximal intestinal regions [11, 12]. This phenomenon likely results from enterohepatic recirculation of PCM‐GLU, which is converted back into PCM before undergoing further hepatic metabolism. In humans, biliary excretion of PCM‐GLU and PCM‐CYS has been reported [30], supporting the existence of enterohepatic recirculation influencing metabolite kinetics.

Fourth, we identified a need to include study‐specific covariates on elimination clearances and the CLH,int for oxidative metabolism, most likely because of higher BMI values observed in Study 2 despite similar total body weights. One possible explanation is the influence of metabolic‐associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD), which is common in patients with obesity, often with varying severity [31]. Additionally, different oral formulations were used between the studies. Study 1 used a suspension, whereas Study 2 used an oral liquid. However, no differences in Fa were detected for different formulations during model development. This is consistent with the physicochemical properties of PCM, as it is known to disperse and dissolve rapidly after oral administration.

In our study, we found that oral PCM leads to faster peak metabolite concentrations, most pronounced for PCM‐CYS and PCM‐MER. Although higher and earlier peaks of these metabolites may raise concerns, it is known that toxicity is related to the amount of reactive metabolite NAPQI formed over time, rather than the magnitude of their concentrations in isolation [32]. The earlier and higher peak concentrations of the oxidative metabolites in individuals with obesity are anticipated to be irrelevant, as the clearance via oxidative metabolism increased proportionally with total PCM clearance alongside increases in both glucuronidation and sulfation [5].

The remaining misspecifications were mainly observed for PCM‐SUL in the intravenous dataset. We attribute this to the fact that, in the original model on the basis of intravenous data (Study 3), a covariate of LBW on plasma clearance of PCM‐SUL was incorporated. Adding LBW or total body weight as a covariate on CLH,int for PCM‐SUL did not resolve this discrepancy in the final model, including both oral and intravenous data. Another, less probable, explanation is that analytical variation differed between datasets. However, this was already accounted for by including an additional theta on the fold‐error of the residual errors. There are a few limitations in our study. First, the collected datasets following oral administration lacked dense sampling within the first hours post‐dose, potentially missing valuable information about the phase during which PCM is absorbed and the metabolites are initially formed. Second, different dosing regimens and oral formulations were used across the included studies, which complicates the interpretation of potential dose‐dependent processes. Although dose‐normalized comparisons were incorporated during modeling, study‐specific factors (e.g., population characteristics and sampling designs) may confound the identification of clear dose‐related trends in metabolism or elimination. Third, the prevalence and severity of MAFLD were not assessed in the cohorts studied. Therefore, it remains unclear what the specific impact of MAFLD is on the formation of different metabolites and how it impacts the overall findings. Fourth, we assumed in our model that all patients had an intact gallbladder and biliary tree. Potentially, previous cholecystectomy may influence the enterohepatic recirculation of PCM‐GLU. Fifth, we found a ratio of CLint,G to CLint,H of 0.00474, which was comparable to the ratio reported for CYP3A4 using midazolam as probe substrate [15]. However, on the basis of current evidence, intestinal CYP3A4 expression is far more prominent than intestinal CYP2E1 expression [24], with hepatic CYP3A4 expression being reported as only twice that of CYP2E1 in humans [33]. Therefore, the true CLG,int to CLH,int ratio for CYP2E1 is likely to be considerably lower than the ratio estimated in our study. As a partial explanation, we hypothesize that the formation of oxidative metabolites of PCM is not mediated by CYP2E1 alone but also involves non‐CYP2E1 pathways, including, for instance, CYP3A4 [1, 34]. Although intestinal metabolism of PCM by CYP3A4 has not been demonstrated previously, we hypothesize that intestinal CYP3A could play a role. Such a contribution would shift the overall CLint,G to CLint,H ratio toward values more similar to those observed for CYP3A4 using midazolam as a probe drug. Nonetheless, this remains uncertain and highly exploratory. Lastly, an evaluation with external datasets to demonstrate model adequacy was not feasible. Given the model's complexity and the integration of three datasets, data‐splitting techniques were neither considered feasible. Instead, we carefully evaluated stratified diagnostics to assess the model's consistency across the different datasets. As indicated, some structural differences were found, most likely attributable to differences in the included populations.

In summary, this study describes PCM and metabolite PK following oral and intravenous administration using a semi‐physiological population PK model that allowed for the quantification of presystemic and systemic metabolism of the different pathways and enterohepatic recirculation. The results demonstrated that oral administration leads to faster metabolite formation, particularly through oxidative metabolism. This model could be used in the future to evaluate and predict special situations such as the influence of overdose or drug interactions (e.g., alcohol). Future PK studies in special populations, such as patients who have undergone metabolic and bariatric surgery, should explicitly evaluate both oral and intravenous PCM administration.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this semi‐physiological population PK model, both hepatic and intestinal presystemic metabolism of PCM were characterized, along with enterohepatic recirculation of PCM‐GLU and its subsequent deglucuronidation back to PCM. Oral administration of PCM results in faster and more extensive metabolite formation. These mechanistic insights are valuable not only for understanding PCM PK but could also support future PK evaluations of other drugs extensively metabolized via multiple routes.

Figure S1: Normalized prediction distribution errors (NPDE) versus time plots for PCM, PCM‐GLU, PCM‐SUL, PCM‐CYS, and PCM‐MER for the population PK model on the basis of the original model of Van Rongen et al. [5] with oral absorption depot. The plots indicate overprediction of the metabolites PCM‐GLU, PCM‐SUL and PCM‐CYS & PCM‐MER, and underprediction of PCM concentrations following oral administration. PCM = paracetamol, PCM‐CYS + PCM‐MER = combined PCM‐mercapturate and PCM‐cysteine, PCM‐GLU = PCM‐glucuronide, PCM‐SUL = PCM‐sulfate, PK = pharmacokinetic.

Figure S2: Normalized prediction distribution errors (NPDE) versus time plots after incorporating presystemic hepatic and intestinal clearance through reparameterization into hepatic and intestinal blood flow and their respective intrinsic hepatic and intestinal clearances, stratified per dataset. The plots show substantial improvement, especially for the oral datasets. PCM = paracetamol, PCM‐CYS + PCM‐MER = combined PCM‐mercapturate and PCM‐cysteine, PCM‐GLU = PCM‐glucuronide, PCM‐SUL = PCM‐sulfate.

Figure S3: Goodness‐of‐fit plots of the final semi‐physiological population PK model: observed versus individual predicted concentrations. The plots are stratified by compound and study. PCM = paracetamol, PCM‐CYS + PCM‐MER = combined PCM‐mercapturate and PCM‐cysteine, PCM‐GLU = PCM‐glucuronide, PCM‐SUL = PCM‐sulfate, PK = pharmacokinetic.

Figure S4: AUC0‐6 at steady‐state following four times 1000 mg daily, simulated for male individuals with different body weights. Their respective lean body weights are 50.6 and 71.5 kg. AUC = area under the time‐curve, IV = intravenous, PCM = paracetamol, PCM‐CYS + PCM‐MER = combined PCM‐mercapturate and PCM‐cysteine, PCM‐GLU = PCM‐glucuronide, PCM‐SUL = PCM‐sulfate.
